2023_007_academic_data_boe_dec_12_2023_v.paragraph: Student Assessment Data, a 27-slide presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education in December 2023, reviews the measures the district tracks consistently over time: the SAT Suite of Assessments (SAT 11 and PSAT 8), M-STEP 3-7, instructional benchmarking tools (Fountas & Pinnell for ELA K-5, Common Lit for ELA 6-12, and NWEA for math 6-Algebra 1), and exit data from Advanced Placement assessments and graduation rate. The celebrations section reports an International Academy East IB diploma acquisition rate of 72% for 2023 against a global acquisition rate of 75-78%, AP Honor Roll recognition for Athens High School and Troy High School, and a Troy College and Career High School four-year graduation rate that increased from 38% to 63% from 2017/18 to 2021/22 while the student dropout rate decreased from 23% to 3%.
2023_007_academic_data_boe_dec_12_2023_v.page:
**Purpose and scope**
Board meeting presentation titled Student Assessment Data, December 2023, organized around reviewing consistent measures over time.

**Measures reviewed**
- Standardized assessment data: SAT Suite of Assessments, Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT 11), PSAT 8, MSTEP 3-7
- Instructional/benchmarking data: Fountas & Pinnell (ELA K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), NWEA - Math (6-Alg1)
- Exit data: Advanced Placement Assessments, Graduation Rate

**Why SAT 11**
Described as a national norm-referenced assessment with consistent content and structure over time (unlike MSTEP/MEAP variance), a leading collegiate admissions assessment, and part of a suite with linkages from grade 8 to grade 11. It is said to show programmatic impact over time, comparison data at state/county/school/student-group level, and transparency in the work ahead. Charted slides cover SAT Grade 11 results and Oakland County performance on SAT 11 EBRW and SAT 11 Math shown with ED (economically disadvantaged) status.

**Subcategory analysis**
Each assessment has subcategories that allow deeper program assessment and review of trends over time in narrower areas of instruction; the deck states that at the system level this data is not useful for addressing specific student learning needs. Math subcategories defined: Heart of Algebra (linear equations, systems of linear equations, linear functions), Passport to Advanced Math (structure of expressions, analyzing/manipulating/rewriting expressions, complex equations, interpreting and building functions), and Problem Solving and Data Analysis (ratios, percentages, proportional reasoning, graphical relationships, statistical data). EBRW subcategories defined: Command of Evidence, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions, and Words in Context. Subcategory comparison charts use a color key of Green for Proficient or Advanced, Yellow for Partially Proficient, and Red for Not Proficient.

**Math benchmarking: PSAT 8 and NWEA**
With the new K-8 math curriculum, PSAT 8 Math performance will serve as one data set for understanding student growth over time. NWEA will be introduced this winter as a second data set for math performance, replacing district-created benchmark assessments; it is administered during the school day in the student's math class and is a norm-referenced, computer-adaptive, nationally administered assessment. The district is engaged in program evaluation in partnership with Illustrative Math. PSAT 8 subcategory comparison slides cover Math and Evidence Based Reading & Writing.

**MSTEP 3-8**
MSTEP (3-7) and PSAT 8 ELA and math data allow tracking of student cohorts over time. The pandemic disrupted the 19/20 and 20/21 data sets, and the spring 2022 assessments form a new baseline. MSTEP supports comparison with other districts but is described as less useful for program assessment because it covers only the last three years of elementary and the first two years of middle school, and does not permit the same level of consistent drill-down. Slides show Oakland County performance for ELA MSTEP 3-8 and Math MSTEP 3-8.

**Celebrations**

International Academy East - IB Diploma Acquisition Rate:

| Year | % Diploma Acquisition |
|---|---|
| 2023 | 72% |
| 2022 | 88% |
| 2021 | 87% |
| 2020 | 90% |
| 2019 | 82% |

Global Acquisition Rate 75-78%.

AP Honor Roll recognition went to Athens High School and Troy High School, using the metrics College Culture (percent of the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score), College Credit (percent who scored 3 or higher on any AP Exam), and College Optimization (percent who took 5 or more AP Exams with at least 1 taken in 9th or 10th grade).

**Troy College and Career High School**
Over the last 4 years the district committed resources to reimagining TCCHS programming: new facility, new leadership, new vision; focus on belonging and flexibility in curriculum; elevation of student voice and choice; and a smaller, adaptive, supportive environment. From 2017/18 to 2021/22 the 4-year graduation rate increased from 38% to 63% and the student dropout rate decreased from 23% to 3%.
2023_007_academic_data_boe_dec_12_2023_v.verbose:
Student Assessment Data was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its December 2023 board meeting as a 27-slide deck (file version v2, meeting date December 12, 2023). Its organizing frame is stated on slide 2 as Reviewing Consistent Measures Over Time, and it groups the district's measures into three categories. Standardized assessment data comprises the SAT Suite of Assessments, the Scholastic Aptitude Test at grade 11 (SAT 11), PSAT 8, and MSTEP for grades 3-7. Instructional and benchmarking data comprises Fountas & Pinnell for ELA in grades K-5, Common Lit for ELA in grades 6-12, and NWEA for math from grade 6 through Algebra 1. Exit data comprises Advanced Placement assessments and graduation rate.

Rationale for SAT 11. Slide 3 sets out why the district anchors its reporting on the grade 11 SAT. It is a national norm-referenced assessment; it has consistent content and structure over time, which the deck contrasts with MSTEP/MEAP variance; it is a leading collegiate admissions assessment; and it belongs to a suite of assessments with linkages running from grade 8 to grade 11. The deck says the assessment shows programmatic impact over time, provides comparison data at the state, county, school, and student-group level, and offers transparency in the work ahead. Slide 4 is headed SAT Grade 11. Slides 5 and 6 present Oakland County Performance for SAT 11 EBRW with ED and Oakland County Performance for SAT 11 Math with ED respectively, displaying county results alongside economically disadvantaged status; the underlying figures appear in charts rather than in the extracted text.

Using data to inform instruction. Slide 7 introduces a section on instructional use of the data. Slide 8, SAT/PSAT Subcategory Data, states that each assessment (SAT/EBRW) has subcategories that allow the district to dig deeper into program assessment, that this level of data is reviewed to understand trends over time in more narrow and focused areas of instruction, and that from the system level this data is not useful for addressing specific student learning needs.

SAT math subcategory definitions. Slide 9 reproduces College Board definitions. Heart of Algebra questions focus on mastery of linear equations, systems of linear equations, and linear functions, with the ability to analyze and create linear equations, inequalities, and functions described as essential for success in college and career, as is fluency in solving linear equations and systems. Passport to Advanced Math questions cover topics important to master before studying advanced math, chief among them understanding the structure of expressions and the ability to analyze, manipulate, and rewrite these expressions, along with reasoning with more complex equations and interpreting and building functions. Problem Solving and Data Analysis covers using ratios, percentages, and proportional reasoning to solve problems in real-world situations including science and social science contexts, describing relationships shown graphically, and analyzing statistical data, described as being quantitatively literate and demonstrating command of math that resonates through college courses, career training programs, and everyday life. Slide 10 carries the SAT Subcategory Comparison for Math with a color key: Green for Proficient or Advanced, Yellow for Partially Proficient, Red for Not Proficient.

SAT Evidence Based Reading and Writing subcategory definitions. Slide 11 defines four categories. Command of Evidence includes questions focused on the best evidence for a specified conclusion (Reading Test), interpreting data presented in informational graphics such as tables, graphs, and charts and drawing connections between words and data (Reading Test and Writing and Language Test), understanding how the author of an argument uses or fails to use evidence to support claims (Reading Test), and revising a passage to clarify main ideas, strengthen support, or sharpen focus (Writing and Language Test). Expression of Ideas questions on the Writing and Language Test focus on refining the substance of a writer's message through topic development, organization, and effective language use in relation to the writer's purpose, addressing rhetorical aspects of the passages. Standard English Conventions questions require editing passages for sentence structure, usage, and punctuation. Words in Context asks students to consider the meaning and role of words and phrases as used in particular passages, covering interpreting words and phrases in context, analyzing word choice rhetorically, and making effective use of language. Slide 12 presents the SAT Subcategory Comparison for Evidence Based Reading & Writing with the same green/yellow/red proficiency key.

Math benchmarking with PSAT 8 and NWEA. Slides 13 and 14 address math benchmarking. As the district moves forward with its new K-8 math curriculum, it will use PSAT 8 math performance as one data set to help understand student growth over time. This winter the district will introduce NWEA as a second data set for student performance in math, replacing district-created benchmark assessments. NWEA assessments are given during the school day, during the student's math class, and NWEA is described as a norm-referenced, computer-adaptive assessment given nationally. The district is engaged in program evaluation in partnership with Illustrative Math. Slide 15 gives the PSAT 8 Subcategory Comparison for Math and slide 16 the PSAT 8 Subcategory Comparison for Evidence Based Reading & Writing, both with the green/yellow/red proficiency key.

Oakland County performance and MSTEP. Slide 17 opens a section on Oakland County performance data. Slide 18 addresses MSTEP 3-8: MSTEP (3-7) and PSAT 8 ELA and math data allow the district to track the performance of student cohorts over time; the pandemic disrupted the 19/20 and 20/21 data sets; and the district has a new baseline to grow from beginning with the spring 2022 assessments. MSTEP data lets the district see how it performs in comparison with other districts, but is described as not as useful for program assessment because it encompasses only the last three years of elementary and the first two years of middle school, and the district is not able to drill down with the same level of consistency in MSTEP. Slide 19 shows Oakland County Performance for ELA MSTEP 3-8 and slide 20 Oakland County Performance for Math MSTEP 3-8.

Celebrations. Slide 21 introduces the celebrations section. Slide 22 covers the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme. Slide 23 gives the International Academy East IB Diploma Acquisition Rate by year: 2023 at 72%, 2022 at 88%, 2021 at 87%, 2020 at 90%, and 2019 at 82%, with a note that the Global Acquisition Rate is 75-78%.

Advanced Placement. Slides 24 and 25 cover Advanced Placement courses and the AP Honor Roll, naming Athens High School and Troy High School. The Honor Roll definitions are given: College Culture is the percent of students in the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score; College Credit is the percent of students in the graduating class who scored 3 or higher on any AP Exam in high school; and College Optimization is the percent of students in the graduating class who took 5 or more AP Exams in high school where at least 1 exam was taken in 9th or 10th grade. The slide adds that research finds 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5 such courses in high school, and that the Honor Roll also recognizes schools that encourage students earlier on their AP journey so as not to overload them with AP courses in their junior and senior years.

Troy College and Career High School. Slides 26 and 27 close the deck on graduation rate at Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS). Over the last 4 years the district committed resources to reimagining the programming at TCCHS, citing a new facility, new leadership, and new vision; a focus on belonging and flexibility in curriculum; elevation of student voice and choice; and the opportunity to learn and grow in a smaller, adaptive, supportive environment. The final slide reports that from 2017/18 to 2021/22 the TCCHS 4-year graduation rate increased from 38% to 63% and the student dropout rate decreased from 23% to 3%.

2023_008_board_self_evaluation_template_.paragraph: Troy School District Board of Education Self-Evaluation for the 2022-2023 school year is a blank rating instrument distributed to trustees ahead of a board workshop. It was developed from the concepts and language of Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan's text The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together, and is organized around six areas the authors identify as central to high-functioning school boards: Coherence, a Governance Mindset, Systems Thinking, Strategic Focus, Deep Learning, and Managing Manner. Trustees rate both the board as a whole and themselves on each attribute using a 4-to-1 scale, add a summary gestalt rating per section, and propose 1 or 2 concrete improvement actions for the next 12 months.
2023_008_board_self_evaluation_template_.page:
**Document type**
Blank self-evaluation template for the Troy School District Board of Education covering the 2022-2023 school year; no completed ratings or narrative responses appear in the file.

**Source and purpose**
The form was developed from the concepts and language established by Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan in The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together. Its stated purpose is to reflect on performance as a board and as individual trustees over the past 12 months and to use that introspection to develop concrete actions for improving performance as a team over the next 12 months. Whenever possible, attribute language is pulled directly from the text. Completed forms are to be brought to a board workshop, where board ratings will guide a constructive discussion.

**Rating scale**
| Rating | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 4 | A foundational strength of this board |
| 3 | Generally good |
| 2 | Needs improvement |
| 1 | A critical weakness of this board |

Each attribute is rated twice, once in a column headed The Board and once in a column headed Me. At the end of each section trustees give a summary or gestalt rating for the section as a whole, which the directions note does not need to be a mathematical average.

**Sections**
- Section 1: Coherence (Individuals' Shared Depth of Understanding about the Nature of the Work) - attributes numbered 1 through 15
- Section 2: Governance Mindset (Core Understanding of the Basic Principles of Governance) - attributes numbered 1 through 15
- Section 3: Strategic Focus - attributes numbered 1 through 6
- Section 4: Systems Thinking - attributes numbered 1 through 4
- Section 5: Deep Learning - attributes numbered 1 through 9
- Section 6: Managing Manner - attributes numbered 1 through 8

Each section is followed by a prompt for 1-2 ideas for improving performance in that area over the next 12 months, expressed in terms of positive, concrete actions or procedural changes.

**Representative attribute content**
Coherence items address depth of understanding of the work, emotional commitment such that the board owns rather than observes the strategic vision, reliability and competence as the basis of trust, confidentiality regarding personnel and closed session content, avoidance of representing specific constituencies or single-issue agendas, willingness to compromise in support of unity of purpose, abiding by policy even after voting against a resolution, and avoiding intervention at the administrative level on behalf of constituents. Governance Mindset items address a shared moral imperative of learning for all students, acting as a cohesive unified team, moving forward after votes are taken, avoiding surface politics, leading from the middle, tracking measurable outcomes, actively tracking the district budget, and keeping constituents informed. Strategic Focus items address limiting questions about implementation tactics to scheduled oversight reviews, agendas focused on educational and student issues, avoiding micro-management, and staying on the what of governance (steering the boat) rather than the how of management (rowing the boat). Systems Thinking items contrast a wide-angle macro lens with a telephoto micro lens and address unintended consequences. Deep Learning items address the board as a group of learners, preparation for meetings, policies supporting global competencies (character, citizenship, collaboration, communication, creativity, critical thinking), confidence in administration-supplied information, and regular purposeful school visits. Managing Manner items address modeling behavior Troy kids should emulate, patience and respect in meetings, the primacy of impact over intent in public statements, empathetic listening, and not taking differences personally.
2023_008_board_self_evaluation_template_.verbose:
Troy School District Board of Education Self-Evaluation, 2022-2023 School Year, is a blank assessment instrument circulated to trustees in advance of a board workshop; the copy in the record contains the full instrument with no ratings entered and no narrative responses.

Introduction and provenance. The evaluation form was developed from the concepts and language established by Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan as set forth in their text The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together. The stated purpose of the assessment is to reflect on performance as a board and as individual trustees over the past 12 months and then to use that introspection to develop concrete actions for improving performance as a team over the next 12 months. The introduction states that Campbell and Fullan identified six key areas central to high-functioning school boards across the US: Coherence, a Governance Mindset, Systems Thinking, Strategic Focus, Deep Learning, and Managing Manner. The assessment is organized around those six areas, with individual attributes identified in the authors' research as key contributors to success in each area; wherever possible the attribute language is pulled directly from the text. Trustees are told their immediate task is to assess the TSD Board and their own performance on each attribute and use that assessment to guide suggestions for the team's future improvement, and that board ratings on the form will be used as a guide for a constructive discussion at the workshop, so the form should be completed and readily available when the board meets.

Directions and rating scale. Focusing only on experience over the past 12 months, each respondent rates both the board as a whole and then themselves on each attribute using a four-point scale: 4, a foundational strength of this board; 3, generally good; 2, needs improvement; and 1, a critical weakness of this board. At the end of each section the respondent provides a summary rating for the section as a whole; the directions specify that this does not need to be a mathematical average but instead more of a gestalt after thinking through the section. Finally, respondents brainstorm 1 or 2 concrete ways the board could improve in each area over the next 12 months, expressed in terms of positive, concrete actions or procedural changes that could be implemented. The response tables carry two columns, The Board and Me, and each section closes with paired Section Summary/Gestalt Rating rows.

Section 1: Coherence (Individuals' Shared Depth of Understanding about the Nature of the Work), attributes numbered 1 through 15. The attributes are: as individuals, trustees have a depth of understanding about the nature of the work; individual trustees demonstrate an emotional commitment to the work of the district, that is, the board owns the strategic vision rather than observes it; individual trustees actively reinforce a culture of trust through action, namely reliability (I keep my word) and competence (I am skilled at follow-through); trustees believe the motivations and inherent beliefs of other trustees are honorable, ethical, and honest; individual trustees maintain confidentiality rules relating to personnel and closed session content; trustees interact on a continuous basis, sorting out differences and arriving at a common understanding that guides and reflects the actions of the district; as individuals, trustees recognize and reinforce the intrinsic impact and power in trustees working together as a single board entity; individual trustees effectively reconcile their core values and beliefs with the development of the board's shared moral imperative and board strategic goals; individual trustees avoid representing specific constituencies, instead focusing on the district's systemwide purpose and work; individual trustees avoid single-issue agendas; trustees remain open to different priorities held by other trustees; as individuals, trustees show a willingness to compromise as long as a decision reinforces the board's unity of purpose; because the district is governed by policy, individual trustees avoid damaging the ability of the board to govern and the district to carry out its mission by abiding by policies even when they vote against a resolution and do not undermine the implementation of the board's policy; as individuals, trustees avoid intervening at the administrative level to solve a problem for constituents; and individual trustees believe the motivations and inherent beliefs of the administration are honorable, ethical, and honest.

Section 2: Governance Mindset (Core Understanding of the Basic Principles of Governance), attributes numbered 1 through 15. The attributes are: the board shows a unity of purpose driven by a shared moral imperative, a relentless commitment to the learning of all students with no exceptions (all children will achieve, all children will have quality teachers, all children will be in a safe, healthy learning environment); the board acts as a cohesive, unified team working together to create a common vision driven by a shared moral imperative rather than a collection of individuals each with his or her own agenda and vision voting on unrelated issues; the board strives for common ground even when there are deep differences and difficulties; rather than strive for group agreement, the board works to make sure there is enough interaction and adult learning going on that some differences are resolved, new shared meanings are achieved, and remaining differences are understood; once votes are taken, the board moves forward to the next issue, leaving behind any discord or hurt feelings; the board avoids surface politics (a narrow view preoccupied with single hot-button issues) and instead focuses on deeper governance (broad consideration of diverse views focused on its unity of purpose); the board strives to lead from the middle by interpreting state and federal policy, working laterally with other districts and regional entities, and liberating those below within the district to do the right work; the board always keeps the focus of its energy on students and learning rather than administrative tasks; the board takes into account diverse views relative to implementation of new policies; the board builds and maintains a strong governance infrastructure for the district; the board supports staff and creates a positive organizational culture; the board holds the district organization accountable to the community it serves; the board tracks measurable outcomes that mark progress and attainment; the board actively tracks the district budget; and the board keeps constituents informed and up to date on the work of the district.

Section 3: Strategic Focus, attributes numbered 1 through 6. The attributes are: the board approaches responsibilities with a clear focus on achieving the strategic outcomes it desires; the board limits its questions of district implementation tactics to scheduled oversight reviews or essential discussions so that administrative issues do not supplant the strategic work of the board; board meeting agendas are more focused on educational and student issues than on administrative work; while maintaining healthy accountability, the board does not micro-manage by intruding into the daily fray of administrative or instructional roles within the district; the board remains focused on the what of governance (steering the boat) versus the how of management (rowing the boat); and the board stays focused on long-term strategic outcomes versus short-term tactical, administrative objectives.

Section 4: Systems Thinking, attributes numbered 1 through 4. The attributes are: the board acts at a macro level, focused on connected, holistic solutions and allocation of scarce resources tied to the district's strategic plan (a wide-angle lens with strong peripheral vision) rather than making micro-level, immediate, tactical decisions (a telephoto lens with sharp focus on one issue); the board consistently takes a broad, systemic view of the district; the board takes the time and effort to step back from solving immediate problems in order to explore and understand broader patterns and the interdependency of issues within the district contributing to that problem; and the board takes the time and effort to think about unintended consequences of its decisions, including how decisions designed to assist one student population or one area of the district might potentially impact another part of the district negatively.

Section 5: Deep Learning, attributes numbered 1 through 9. The attributes are: the board itself strives to be a group of learners, going outside its comfort zone to gain new understanding; individual trustees engage in deep learning on major educational issues and challenges facing the students served; individual trustees come to meetings fully prepared; the board sets policies that ensure students will develop global competencies and skills required for living in a complex, unpredictable world (character, citizenship, collaboration, communication, creativity, and critical thinking); the board drives deep learning within the district; the board has confidence in the quality and validity of information provided by the administration; the board completes regular, purposeful visits to schools; the board collectively discusses strategies for addressing credibility concerns within the district; and all information gathering by board trustees reinforces openness, teamwork, and trust within the district.

Section 6: Managing Manner, attributes numbered 1 through 8. The attributes are: the board consistently models behavior the district wants Troy kids to emulate; trustee behavior in meetings demonstrates patience, understanding, respect, common courtesy, and sense of humor; trustees recognize that the impact of their public statements is all that matters and intent does not; trustees listen to each other with their ears, eyes, undivided attention, and heart, adopting an empathetic approach focused on an intent to understand; trustees reserve judgment on each other; trustee positions stay focused on content, not on the behavior or style of other trustees; trustees treat each other with respect; and trustees do not take differences personally.

2023_010_november_2023_accountability_re.paragraph: The November 2023 Accountability Report presents Troy School District's Project 2026 Blueprint progress to the Board of Education, structured around the four World Class for All pillars, each with objectives, key results, celebrations, challenges, and recommendations for the period June through November 2023. Under the Green pillar (Early Childhood to Career), 2023-24 early childhood enrollment is reported as Tuition at 240 max, GSRP at 98 (a 16-student increase) launching at Hill, Morse, Troy Union and Wass, Strong Beginnings serving 14 TSD students in a free three-year-old program, PreK at 100 max, and ECP at 96 max. Other milestones include the Fall 2023 launch of Portrait of a Learner, a Career Accelerator Program launched 11/8/23, and an Early Middle College partnership with LTU.
2023_010_november_2023_accountability_re.page:
**Framework**
Project 2026 Blueprint, presented at district and school level for Troy, with a redesign process described as See, Engage, Act. The accountability plan states that the World Class for All pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results.

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, providing more students with access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science, connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors, and include partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers, and other stakeholders enabling quality work-based learning, credentials, and/or college credit.
Key results (updated November 2023): increase access to high-quality preschool; focus on meaningful transition from preschool to kindergarten; monitoring of preschool impact on achievement data, access across the district, ELD in kindergarten, ELD performance, and PreK performance; Portrait of a Learner launch Fall 2023; enhance career readiness K-12; expanding the Student Portfolio Project.

2023-24 Early Childhood Enrollment:

| Program | Figure |
|---|---|
| Tuition | 240 Max |
| GSRP | 98 (16 student increase), launching at Hill, Morse, Troy Union & Wass |
| Strong Beginnings | 14 TSD students, free 3-year-old program |
| PreK | 100 Max (increased section from 22-23) |
| ECP | 96 max |

Celebrations also include career readiness engagement K-8 partnered with media specialists and Maker Space growth, expanding maker-centered learning spaces to high school, Early Middle College with LTU, a Business Round Table, the Career Accelerator Program launched 11/8/23, launch of a digital learning portfolio for grades 3-9, student-led learning with middle school innovation coaches, media specialists and 6-8 English teachers, and ties to Xello for future-ready career discussions.
Challenges: recruitment and retention of highly qualified staff; identifying barriers to preschool access; alignment of media implements and Maker Space with career readiness (training time and consistency/buy-in); shifting the stigma of career readiness; supporting secondary building leaders; connecting Portrait of a Learner to the current strategic plan.
Recommendations: ongoing preschool recruitment; messaging career readiness alongside academic planning and college readiness; business partnerships for work-based learning; expanding TSD Learning Portfolios to all students and parents in grades 3-9; prioritizing digital citizenship K-12; expanding embedded career readiness K-12; jumpstarting computer science K-12 curriculum collaboration with the Oakland Schools Computer Science team; launching Portrait of a Learner to the TSD community.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives: ensure a focus on equity and well-being; fund additional investments to support the needs of the whole child; elevate focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency district wide; assess needs and act to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.
Celebrations/key results: SEL curriculum expansion through pilots (Everyday Speech, Navigate 360, Restorative Practices); SEL-focused programming including Unified Sports, Advisory, Peer to Peer, tiered intervention, WEB, and Character.org; transforming adult SEL through affinity groups, a Dare to Lead series, professional learning, and climate and culture capture; Learning to Impact leadership professional learning (ILT); elevating student experience through a Student Equity Council structure/model and Hanover.
Challenges/recommendations: community engagement and partnerships; aligned structures; equity teamwork across buildings; SEL curriculum and instruction; MTSS consistency; Hanover recommendations to deepen equity professional learning, focus heavily on bullying, and prioritize diversity resources district wide including gender identities and expression; continued social work, psychologist and counseling support in all buildings; more cohesive relationships and support across buildings.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning**
Objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS); improve technology access for students and families with quality training; pursue global best practices in all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); assess the need and act on upgraded facilities. Sections cover furniture, playgrounds, and student designs and input, with student quotes about places to climb and play sports, rockers, movable furniture, and shade and nature. Curriculum and pedagogy work includes job-embedded learning in mathematics K-Algebra, math parent nights at each level, 10th grade ELA curriculum development, high school physics curriculum development, job-embedded learning for media specialists with partner Edward Clapp, and growing digital portfolios. MTSS work includes a partnership with New Solutions K-12, elementary benchmark monitoring and math capacity, secondary collaboration practices, and a partnership with Solution Tree. Challenges include collaboration time, coordinating implementation, substitute teacher coverage, and building capacity of all staff.

**Gold Pillar - Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families**
Objectives: improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, and support current educators; provide job-embedded professional learning for all staff; provide professional learning for staff, community, and students to co-design impactful experiences for the OneTroy community.
Key results: job-embedded learning for staff; a parent learning series hosted with Celebrate Hope; use of early release days for collaborative teacher team conversations about student learning; launch of a weekly district-wide newsletter.
Challenges/recommendations: continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; investigation into attracting experienced staff from outside the district; retention strategies; community partnerships; collaboration among departments within Sub Cabinet; leadership cohorts; a new teacher learning series.

**Closing**
A What's Next slide quotes that the world's best school systems ensure all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system, with leaders clarifying a few very specific non-negotiables while encouraging autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation.
2023_010_november_2023_accountability_re.verbose:
The November 2023 Accountability Report was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at the November 14, 2023 meeting as a 27-slide deck titled Project 2026 Blueprint, covering district and school level for Troy. Early slides frame the work: Clarifying Our Foundation, a redesign process described as See, Engage, Act, and an Accountability Plan slide stating that the World Class for All pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. The body of the deck steps through four color-coded pillars, each with objectives, key results and celebrations, challenges, and recommendations for the June through November 2023 reporting period.

Green Pillar: Early Childhood to Career. The objectives are to continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds, and to expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students. The pathways objective is stated as providing more students with access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science; connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors; and include partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers, and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality, work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

Green pillar key results, updated November 2023, are: increase access to high quality preschool; focus on meaningful transition from preschool to kindergarten; monitoring, specifically the impact of preschool on achievement data, monitoring access across the district, monitoring ELD in kindergarten, performance of ELD, and performance of PreK; Portrait of a Learner with a launch in Fall 2023; enhance career readiness K-12; and expanding the Student Portfolio Project.

The Green pillar June-November 2023 celebrations slide reports 2023-24 early childhood enrollment figures: Tuition at 240 max; GSRP at 98, described as a 16 student increase, launching at Hill, Morse, Troy Union and Wass; Strong Beginnings serving 14 TSD students in a free 3-year-old program; PreK at 100 max, an increased section from 22-23; and ECP at 96 max. The same slide lists access and achievement data; Portrait of a Learner with a Fall 2023 launch; career readiness engagement opportunities K-8 partnered with media specialists and Maker Space growth; expanding maker-centered learning spaces to the high school level; continuing to prioritize post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12; Early Middle College with LTU; a Business Round Table; the Career Accelerator Program launched 11/8/23; launch of a digital learning portfolio for grades 3-9; student-led learning opportunities with middle school innovation coaches, media specialists, and 6-8 English teachers; and ties to Xello and future-ready career discussions with students and the portfolio.

Green pillar challenges for June-November 2023 are recruitment and retention of highly qualified staff; identifying barriers to preschool access; alignment of media implements and Maker Space with career readiness, specifically training time and consistency or buy-in; mindshifting the stigma of career readiness to help prioritize relevance to learning in classrooms; supporting secondary building leaders to embed career readiness initiatives in classrooms and beyond; and Portrait of a Learner, leveraging and embracing connection to the current strategic plan.

Green pillar recommendations are to continue ongoing preschool recruitment and increasing access; continue to prioritize messaging career readiness as a tool for students aligned with academic planning and college readiness with administrators, teachers, and counselors; continue to focus on business partnerships to enhance work-based learning opportunities for all high school students; expand TSD Learning Portfolios to all students and parents in grades 3-9; prioritize digital citizenship for K-12; continue to expand embedded career readiness initiatives K-12 via media and elective classes; jumpstart TSD's computer science K-12 curriculum collaboration with the Oakland Schools Computer Science team; and launch Portrait of a Learner to the TSD community.

Red Pillar: Equity and Well-Being. The objectives are ensuring a focus on equity and well-being; funding additional investments to support the needs of the whole child; an elevated focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency district wide; and assessing needs and taking action to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities. Celebrations and key results for June-November 2023 are SEL curriculum expansion through continued pilots (Everyday Speech, Navigate 360, Restorative Practices); SEL-focused programming including Unified Sports, Advisory, Peer to Peer Programs, Tiered Intervention, WEB, and Character.org; transforming adult SEL through affinity groups using a Dare to Lead series, professional learning, and climate and culture capture; Learning to Impact leadership professional learning (ILT); and elevating student experience through a Student Equity Council structure/model and Hanover. A further Red pillar slide is headed Student Voice, Agency, and Belonging.

Red pillar challenges and recommendations include community engagement and partnerships; encouraging and implementing aligned structures; equity teamwork across buildings; SEL curriculum and instruction; MTSS consistency; and Hanover recommendations to dive deeper into professional learning for staff in the areas of equity, focus heavily on issues of bullying, and prioritize diversity in resources district wide and in gender identities and expression. The pillar also calls for continued social work, psychologist and counseling support in all buildings and work toward more cohesive relationships and levels of support across all buildings.

Blue Pillar: Deep Learning. The objectives are to create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children; to improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning; to continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); and to assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world-class learning environment in all school communities. Dedicated slides cover Furniture, Playgrounds, and Student Designs and Input for Playgrounds and Furniture, the last carrying student quotations: a request for places to climb and play sports to get energy out; a preference for rockers because a student can rock on them and sit on the carpet to read, making it easy to concentrate and comfortable; a statement that a favorite is something the student can move with; and a request for shade and nice places to relax with friends in nature.

Blue pillar curriculum and pedagogy work comprises job-embedded learning for all teachers in mathematics K-Algebra; math parent nights at each level, either occurred or planned; continuing to develop the 10th grade ELA curriculum; continuing to develop the high school physics curriculum; job-embedded learning for media specialists with partner Edward Clapp; and continuing to grow digital portfolios for students to document learning over time. The multi-tiered systems of support slide describes a partnership with New Solutions K-12, a review of current systems of support, developing a guiding coalition, and planning for implementation of recommendations; elementary MTSS work continuing to monitor benchmark data, continuing to develop capacity in math, and solidifying tier-one instruction in all classrooms; and secondary MTSS work developing collaboration practices across schools, building MTSS teams meeting regularly to support student needs, considering system data to be utilized, and a partnership with Solution Tree to build instructional leadership capacity. Blue pillar challenges are regular time for teachers to collaborate; coordinating implementation across teams of principals, teachers, content areas, and support staff; continuously supporting all content areas; substitute teacher coverage; systemness and building capacity of all staff; and helping staff see connections across content area and level.

Gold Pillar: Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families. The objectives are improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continuing to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and providing professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community. Gold pillar key results are job-embedded learning for staff; a hosted parent learning series with Celebrate Hope; utilizing early release days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning; and the launch of a weekly district-wide newsletter. Gold pillar challenges and recommendations are continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; continued investigation into attracting experienced staff from outside of the district; retention strategies; building community partnerships; continued collaboration among departments within Sub Cabinet; leadership cohorts; and a new teacher learning series.

Closing. The What's Next slide quotes that the world's best school systems ensure that all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system, and that leaders clarify a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system while at the same time encouraging autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation.

2023_011_academic_data_boe_nov_2023_v2.paragraph: Student Assessment Data, presented at the Troy School District Board of Education workshop in November 2023, is a 39-slide review of the measures the district tracks consistently over time, including the SAT Suite (SAT 11 and PSAT 8), MSTEP 3-7, benchmarking through Fountas & Pinnell, Common Lit and NWEA, and exit data from Advanced Placement and graduation rate. Beyond Oakland County comparisons, the deck adds peer district performance analysis for PSAT 8, SAT 11 and MSTEP 3-7, explaining that peer districts are selected outside Oakland County on size, per-pupil economics, performance, and community expectations. Celebrations report an International Academy East IB diploma acquisition rate of 72% in 2023 against a global rate of 75-78%, AP Honor Roll status for Athens and Troy High Schools, and a Troy College and Career High School four-year graduation rate that rose from 38% to 63% from 2017/18 to 2021/22 as the dropout rate fell from 23% to 3%.
2023_011_academic_data_boe_nov_2023_v2.page:
**Occasion**
Board workshop presentation, November 2023 (39 slides), titled Student Assessment Data.

**Measures tracked over time**
- Standardized: SAT Suite of Assessments, Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT 11), PSAT 8, MSTEP 3-7
- Instructional/benchmarking: Fountas & Pinnell (ELA K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), NWEA - Math (6-Alg1)
- Exit: Advanced Placement Assessments, Graduation Rate

**SAT 11 rationale**
A national norm-referenced assessment with consistent content and structure over time (unlike MSTEP/MEAP variance), a leading collegiate admissions assessment, and part of a suite with linkages from grade 8 to 11. It shows programmatic impact over time, comparison data at state/county/school/student group level, and transparency in the work ahead. Four chart slides following SAT Grade 11 are annotated Represents % SED by Building.

**Subcategory analysis**
Subcategories allow deeper program assessment and trend analysis in narrower areas of instruction, though the deck notes this data is not useful at system level for addressing specific student learning needs. Math subcategories defined are Heart of Algebra, Passport to Advanced Math, and Problem Solving and Data Analysis. EBRW subcategories defined are Command of Evidence, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions, and Words in Context. Comparison charts use a key of Green for Proficient or Advanced, Yellow for Partially Proficient, Red for Not Proficient, and appear for both SAT and PSAT 8 in Math and EBRW.

**Math benchmarking**
With the new K-8 math curriculum, PSAT 8 Math performance is one data set for student growth over time. NWEA will be introduced this winter as a second data set, replacing district-created benchmark assessments; it is given during the school day in the student's math class and is norm-referenced, computer adaptive, and administered nationally. Program evaluation is underway in partnership with Illustrative Math.

**MSTEP 3-8**
MSTEP (3-7) and PSAT 8 ELA and math data allow cohort tracking; the pandemic disrupted the 19/20 and 20/21 data sets and spring 2022 provides a new baseline. MSTEP supports cross-district comparison but is less useful for program assessment, covering only the last three years of elementary and the first two years of middle school, without the same consistency of drill-down.

**Oakland County performance**
Slides present Oakland County performance for ELA MSTEP 3-8, Math MSTEP 3-8, PSAT 8, SAT 11, SAT 11 EBRW with ED, and SAT 11 Math with ED, followed by a slide headed Out-performing expectations.

**Peer district comparison**
Peer districts are selected for comparison outside of Oakland County to provide an opportunity to reflect and learn from others. Areas of similarity are size, economics (per pupil), performance/achievement, and community expectations; areas of difference are student need (ELD, SES) and demographics. Peer district performance slides cover PSAT 8 and SAT 11, and MSTEP 3-7.

**Celebrations**

International Academy East - IB Diploma Acquisition Rate:

| Year | % Diploma Acquisition |
|---|---|
| 2023 | 72% |
| 2022 | 88% |
| 2021 | 87% |
| 2020 | 90% |
| 2019 | 82% |

Global Acquisition Rate 75-78%.

AP Honor Roll recognition for Athens High School and Troy High School, defined by College Culture (took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score), College Credit (scored 3 or higher on any AP Exam), and College Optimization (took 5 or more AP Exams with at least 1 in 9th or 10th grade); the deck notes research finding that 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5.

**Troy College and Career High School**
Over the last 4 years the district committed resources to reimagining TCCHS programming, including a new facility, new leadership and new vision, focus on belonging and flexibility in curriculum, elevation of student voice and choice, and a smaller, adaptive, supportive environment. From 2017/18 to 2021/22 the 4-year graduation rate increased from 38% to 63% and the student dropout rate decreased from 23% to 3%.
2023_011_academic_data_boe_nov_2023_v2.verbose:
Student Assessment Data was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at a board workshop in November 2023 (file version v2, meeting date November 14, 2023). The 39-slide deck is the workshop-length companion to the shorter December 2023 board meeting version, sharing its framework but adding Oakland County PSAT 8 and SAT 11 slides, an out-performing expectations slide, and a full peer district comparison section.

Framework. Slide 2, Reviewing Consistent Measures Over Time, lists standardized assessment data as the SAT Suite of Assessments, the Scholastic Aptitude Test at grade 11 (SAT 11), PSAT 8, and MSTEP grades 3-7; instructional and benchmarking data as Fountas & Pinnell for ELA K-5, Common Lit for ELA 6-12, and NWEA for math from grade 6 through Algebra 1; and exit data as Advanced Placement assessments and graduation rate.

Why SAT 11. Slide 3 states the SAT 11 is a national norm-referenced assessment with consistent content and structure over time, contrasted with MSTEP/MEAP variance; that it is a leading collegiate admissions assessment; and that it is part of a suite of assessments with linkages from grade 8 to grade 11. It shows programmatic impact over time, comparison data at the state, county, school, and student-group level, and transparency in the work ahead. Slide 4 is headed SAT Grade 11, and slides 5 through 8 are chart slides each annotated Represents % SED by Building, tying building-level results to the percentage of socioeconomically disadvantaged students.

Using data to inform instruction. Slide 9 opens the instructional-use section and slide 10, SAT/PSAT Subcategory Data, states that each assessment (SAT/EBRW) has subcategories allowing deeper program assessment, that this level of data is reviewed to understand trends over time in more narrow and focused areas of instruction, and that from the system level it is not useful for addressing specific student learning needs.

SAT math subcategory definitions. Slide 11 defines three math subcategories. Heart of Algebra questions focus on mastery of linear equations, systems of linear equations, and linear functions; the ability to analyze and create linear equations, inequalities, and functions is described as essential for success in college and career, as is fluency in solving linear equations and systems. Passport to Advanced Math questions include topics especially important to master before studying advanced math, chief among them understanding the structure of expressions and the ability to analyze, manipulate, and rewrite these expressions, plus reasoning with more complex equations and interpreting and building functions. Problem Solving and Data Analysis includes using ratios, percentages, and proportional reasoning to solve problems in real-world situations including science and social science contexts, describing relationships shown graphically, and analyzing statistical data, framed as quantitative literacy that resonates throughout college courses, career training programs, and everyday life. Slide 12 presents the SAT Subcategory Comparison for Math with the color key Green for Proficient or Advanced, Yellow for Partially Proficient, Red for Not Proficient.

SAT EBRW subcategory definitions. Slide 13 defines four categories. Command of Evidence includes questions focused on the best evidence for a specified conclusion (Reading Test), interpreting data presented in informational graphics such as tables, graphs, and charts and drawing connections between words and data (Reading Test, Writing and Language Test), understanding how the author of an argument uses or fails to use evidence to support claims (Reading Test), and revising a passage to clarify main ideas, strengthen support, or sharpen focus (Writing and Language Test). Expression of Ideas questions on the Writing and Language Test focus on refining the substance of a writer's message through topic development, organization, and effective language use in relation to the writer's purpose, addressing rhetorical aspects of the passages. Standard English Conventions questions require editing passages for sentence structure, usage, and punctuation. Words in Context asks students to consider both the meaning and role of words and phrases as used in particular passages, covering interpreting words and phrases in context, analyzing word choice rhetorically, and making effective use of language. Slide 14 carries the SAT Subcategory Comparison for Evidence Based Reading & Writing with the same proficiency key.

Math benchmarking with PSAT 8 and NWEA. Slides 15 and 16 explain that as the district moves forward with its new K-8 math curriculum it will use PSAT 8 math performance as one data set to help understand student growth over time, and that this winter it will introduce NWEA as a second data set for student performance in math. NWEA will replace district-created benchmark assessments; NWEA assessments are given during the school day, during the student's math class; and NWEA is described as a norm-referenced, computer-adaptive assessment given nationally. The district is engaged in program evaluation in partnership with Illustrative Math. Slide 17 gives the PSAT 8 Subcategory Comparison for Math and slide 18 the PSAT 8 Subcategory Comparison for Evidence Based Reading & Writing, both with the green/yellow/red key.

Oakland County performance and MSTEP. Slide 19 opens the Oakland County performance data section. Slide 20 addresses MSTEP 3-8, stating that MSTEP (3-7) and PSAT 8 ELA and math data allow tracking of student cohort performance over time; that the pandemic disrupted the 19/20 and 20/21 data sets; that a new baseline exists to grow from beginning with the spring 2022 assessments; that MSTEP data allows comparison of district performance with other districts; that MSTEP is not as useful for program assessment because it encompasses only the last three years of elementary and the first two years of middle school; and that the district cannot drill down with the same level of consistency in MSTEP. Slides 21 through 26 present Oakland County Performance for ELA MSTEP 3-8, Math MSTEP 3-8, PSAT 8, SAT 11, SAT 11 EBRW with ED, and SAT 11 Math with ED. Slide 28 is headed Out-performing expectations.

Peer district comparison. Slide 29 opens a Peer District Comparison Data section, and slide 30 explains how peer districts are selected: comparison outside of Oakland County, providing an opportunity to reflect and learn from others. Areas of similarity in these districts are size, economics measured per pupil, performance and achievement, and community expectations. Areas of difference are student need, specifically ELD and SES, and demographics. Slide 31 shows Peer District Performance for PSAT 8 and SAT 11, and slide 32 shows Peer District Performance for MSTEP 3-7.

Celebrations. Slide 33 opens the celebrations section and slide 34 covers the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme. Slide 35 gives the International Academy East IB Diploma Acquisition Rate by year: 2023 at 72%, 2022 at 88%, 2021 at 87%, 2020 at 90%, and 2019 at 82%, with a stated Global Acquisition Rate of 75-78%.

Advanced Placement. Slides 36 and 37 cover Advanced Placement courses and the AP Honor Roll, naming Athens High School and Troy High School. The definitions given are College Culture, the percent of students in the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score; College Credit, the percent of students in the graduating class who scored 3 or higher on any AP Exam in high school; and College Optimization, the percent of students in the graduating class who took 5 or more AP Exams in high school where at least 1 exam was taken in 9th or 10th grade. The slide notes research finding that 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5 such courses in high school, and that the Honor Roll also recognizes schools that encourage students earlier on their AP journey so as not to overload them with AP courses in their junior and senior years.

Troy College and Career High School. Slides 38 and 39 close the deck on graduation rate at Troy College and Career High School. Over the last 4 years the district committed resources to reimagining the programming at TCCHS, citing a new facility, new leadership, and new vision; a focus on belonging and flexibility in curriculum; elevation of student voice and choice; and the opportunity to learn and grow in a smaller, adaptive, supportive environment. The final slide states that from 2017/18 to 2021/22 the TCCHS 4-year graduation rate increased from 38% to 63% and the student dropout rate decreased from 23% to 3%.

2023_012_m091923bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting held September 19, 2023 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, record recognitions, a suicide prevention proclamation, and routine approvals before roughly 80 audience members. President Karl Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. with Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson present and Assistant Superintendent West sitting in for absent Superintendent Machesky; the meeting adjourned at 8:46 p.m. Every recorded vote passed 7 to 0, including the consent agenda covering items A through G and a personnel slate, and Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services John Pagel reported that the District hired 61 new teachers and 11 administrators who are new or new to their position.
2023_012_m091923bdmtg.page:
**Meeting**
Board of Education, Troy, Michigan - Board Meeting Minutes, September 19, 2023, Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; present in addition to Mr. Schmidt were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Assistant Superintendent West sat in for Superintendent Machesky, who was absent. Administrators present were Montante, DiPilato, Pagel, Fulcher, Cross, Young, Griffin, and Milanov. Approximately 80 members of the audience attended. Mr. Schmidt changed the order of the agenda because two student Board Reps had not yet arrived. The meeting adjourned at 8:46 p.m.; minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

**Recognitions**
- TSD Mission Moment: Baker 8th grade student Aryan Khedkar, the final Michigan speller left in the 2023 Scripps National Spelling Bee, who won the Baker Spelling Bee, swept the Oakland County Bee, and reached the finals as one of the final five of the original 231 students competing nationally. He received congratulations and a certificate.
- Student representatives for 2023-2024: Teagan Pruitt (Troy College & Career High School), Nurayda Albeez (International Academy - East), Marlien William (Athens High School), and Jayla Turner (Troy High School).
- All-State athletes, spring 2023, recognized with Mr. Fulcher: Krish Gupta, Vishvaa Ravishankar, Noah Yee, Sanjit Vijay and Darius Whiteside II (Troy High Boys' Track); Erin Humphrey (Troy High Girls' Lacrosse); Grace Zhu, Nika Tananko, Varsha Penumalee and Vienna Thieu (Troy High Girls' Tennis); Lizzie Bultnyck (Troy High Girls' Soccer); Kavitha Gowda (Athens Girls' Tennis); Lauren DeJonckheere (Athens Girls' Soccer).
- Student Spotlight: Thomas Butcher presented the work of 8th grade Boulan Park Middle School student Meera Iyer, who produced a podcast about the District's instrumental music program and received a certificate.
- MASB awards presented by Mr. West: Vital Anne, Award of Distinction (Levels 1 and 2, four advanced CBA classes, minimum 208 education credits); Karl Schmidt, Master Platinum Award (Levels 1-5, 19 advanced classes, minimum 813 education credits); Nancy Philippart, President's Award (Levels 1-6, 29 advanced level classes, minimum 1,383 education credits); and the Board as a whole, Standard of Excellence Award.

**National Suicide Prevention Month proclamation**
Moved by Dr. Wilson, supported by Mr. Hauff, at the request of Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN), recognizing September 2023 as National Suicide Prevention Month. Recitals note World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10; CDC data that each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide; that suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age, the fourth leading cause among people 35 to 54, and the eighth leading cause among people 55 to 64; the roles of NAMI and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988; and OCHN's commitment to being a Zero Suicide organization. Yes: 7, No: 0. Resolution adopted.

**Consent agenda**
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, approving items A through G: Minutes of the August 15, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; Minutes of the August 15, 2023 Closed Session Meeting; Treasurer's Report - July 2023; Athens High School Girls Gymnastics Cooperative Agreement; Troy College & Career High School Course Catalogue; Furniture - Central Office & Services Bldg. Board Rooms; and Cancel November 21, 2023 Board of Education Meeting. Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Personnel**
John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, reported on the hiring process and factors influencing the number of teachers hired each year: retirements/resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status, and student enrollment. The District hired 61 new teachers and 11 administrators new or new to their position. Asked by Mr. Schmidt about vacancies, Mr. Pagel said two social worker positions, one science teacher position, and two special education teacher positions remain to be filled. A slate of new hires was approved on a motion by Mrs. Alic supported by Mrs. Anne, Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Curriculum**
Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, presented on Summer Professional Learning and Summer School, including Principal Retreats, Teaching & Learning Department Retreats, the TSD Literacy Project with over 80 teachers participating, Preschool Literacy and Mathematics Institutes, a free Summer Learning Lab for students entering grades 6-8 using the Stanford design thinking process, Title 1 opportunities such as the Morse Summer Nights reading program, book clubs, writing and art camp, programs for multilingual learners, high school summer school, and special education programs.

**Public communication and other business**
Troy resident Mr. Alex Karpowitsch addressed the Board on livestreaming Board of Education meetings, engaging in dialogue with community speakers, and the recent publishing of test scores. The Board certified Vital Anne, Nicole Wilson, and Karl Schmidt as delegates to the MASB 2023 Delegate Assembly on November 9, 2023, with Matt Haupt as alternate (7-0); approved a delegation of no more than three Board members to the 2024 NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C., January 28-30, 2024 (7-0); and approved a delegation of no more than four Board members to the 2024 NSBA Annual Conference for Public Education Leaders in New Orleans, Louisiana, April 6-8, 2024 (7-0). Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for October 3 at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the next regular meeting for October 17 at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building.
2023_012_m091923bdmtg.verbose:
Minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, Board Meeting of September 19, 2023, held at the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Assistant Superintendent West was sitting in for Superintendent Machesky, who was absent. Also present were administrators Montante, DiPilato, Pagel, Fulcher, Cross, Young, Griffin, and Milanov. There were approximately 80 members of the audience. Mr. Schmidt changed the order of the agenda since two of the student Board Reps had not yet arrived.

TSD Mission Moment. The Board recognized Baker 8th grade student Aryan Khedkar, the final Michigan speller left in the 2023 Scripps National Spelling Bee. Aryan won the Baker Spelling Bee, swept through the Oakland County Bee, dominated at the National Bee, and made it to the finals as one of the final five remaining spellers of the original 231 students competing from across the country. The minutes note that while he did not finish in first place, he inspired the entire oneTROY community, showcased an impressive competitive spirit, and dazzled the judges on a national stage; he received congratulations and a certificate from the Board and will compete again this year.

Student representatives for board meetings. Mr. Schmidt introduced and welcomed the high school student representatives to the Board for the 2023-2024 school year. Teagan Pruitt, Troy College & Career High School, is a senior and four-year veteran of TCC described as a boomerang, a leader who has excelled academically, leads classroom discussions, and pioneered TCC's two Advanced Placement classes, and who plans to attend college, study English Language Arts, earn a teaching certificate, and return to teach at his alma mater. Nurayda Albeez, International Academy - East, is a junior pursuing an International Baccalaureate Diploma who has been part of the Superintendent's Student Advisory Board (SSAB) since freshman year and will serve on the SSAB Executive Committee, is Vice President of Student Government and a former State Officer for the Michigan Health Occupations Students of America (HOSA), has completed over 350 hours of community service, and has been recognized with the President's Volunteer Service Gold Award for the past two years; she is a former Barnard Blue Jay and Baker Bobcat. Marlien William, Athens High School, is a senior and first generation Egyptian-American serving as President of the National Honor Society, Co-President of Key Club, and Co-President of the Superintendent's Student Advisory Board, a member of the Unified Basketball Team for the past three years and of the TSD Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion panel, active at St. Mark Coptic Orthodox Church, who hopes to pursue a dual degree in International Relations and Economics with Spanish and Arabic concentrations and to work for the United States Foreign Service and with the United Nations. Jayla Turner, Troy High School, is a senior serving as Director of Communications for the Troy High School Student Government Executive Board, a member of Mr. Roncone's Principal Student Advisory Board, head mediator for the Peer Mediation program, an active member of the Black Student Union Club, a contributor to the Troy High School Yearbook program, and a varsity athlete in Cheerleading and Softball who has also played Basketball and varsity Track & Field.

All-State athletes, 2023 spring sports. Mr. Fulcher and the Board recognized: Krish Gupta, Senior, Troy High, Boys' Track; Vishvaa Ravishankar, Junior, Troy High, Boys' Track; Noah Yee, Senior, Troy High, Boys' Track; Sanjit Vijay, Senior, Troy High, Boys' Track; Darius Whiteside II, Senior, Troy High, Boys' Track; Erin Humphrey, Junior, Troy High, Girls' Lacrosse; Grace Zhu, Senior, Troy High, Girls' Tennis; Nika Tananko, Junior, Troy High, Girls' Tennis; Varsha Penumalee, Senior, Troy High, Girls' Tennis; Vienna Thieu, Senior, Troy High, Girls' Tennis; Lizzie Bultnyck, Senior, Troy High, Girls' Soccer; Kavitha Gowda, Junior, Athens, Girls' Tennis; and Lauren DeJonckheere, Junior, Athens, Girls' Soccer.

Student Spotlight. The Board introduced the first Student Spotlight of the year, recognizing students for creative achievements in the TSD Creative Guild. Thomas Butcher came to the podium to share the work of 8th grade student Meera Iyer of Boulan Park Middle School, who produced a podcast about the District's instrumental music program; Meera received a certificate from the Board.

National Suicide Prevention Month. Oakland Community Health Network asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with them by approving a proclamation for September as National Suicide Prevention Month at their September board meetings. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff. The recitals state that September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month and is intended to help raise awareness surrounding suicide prevention resources available in the community; that World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10; that suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion, or background; that according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide; that suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age, the fourth leading cause among people 35 to 54 years of age, and the eighth leading cause among people 55 to 64 years of age; that organizations like the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988, work to help individuals in crisis and provide resources on a highly stigmatized topic; that every member of the community should understand that throughout life's struggles all need the occasional reminder that we are all silently fighting our own battles; and that OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization and cultivating a network of providers engaged in the Zero Suicide philosophy. The resolving clause recognizes September 2023 as National Suicide Prevention Month and calls upon individuals, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations, and schools to recommit the state to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention and the need for appropriate and accessible services to assist individuals in crisis. Yes: 7, No: 0. Resolution adopted.

Michigan Association of School Boards awards. Mr. West presented several honors received over the past year. Board Trustee Vital Anne was recognized for achieving the Award of Distinction, which requires completion of Levels 1 and 2, a total of four advanced CBA classes, and a minimum of 208 education credits. President Karl Schmidt received the Master Platinum Award, which requires completion of Levels 1-5, a total of 19 advanced classes, and a minimum of 813 education credits. Representatives from MASB came to the District to present Board Trustee Nancy Philippart with the President's Award, given to those who have completed Levels 1-6, a total of 29 advanced level classes, and a minimum of 1,383 education credits. Mr. West also congratulated the entire Board for earning the Standard of Excellence Award, noting these awards place the Troy Board of Education among a handful of Michigan school district governing bodies demonstrating a true commitment to student achievement and exemplary leadership, and that the Troy community is fortunate to have seven Board members so committed to life-long learning and positive policy making. There were no additions and deletions and no public communication on agenda items.

General consent agenda. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D, E, F, and G: Minutes of the August 15, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; Minutes of the August 15, 2023 Closed Session Meeting; Treasurer's Report - July 2023; Athens High School Girls Gymnastics Cooperative Agreement; Troy College & Career High School Course Catalogue; Furniture - Central Office & Services Bldg. Board Rooms; and Cancel November 21, 2023 Board of Education Meeting. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Personnel and staffing update. John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, reported on the District's hiring process and the factors influencing the number of teachers hired each year, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status, and student enrollment. This year the District hired 61 new teachers and 11 administrators who are either new or new to their position. Mr. Schmidt asked whether all positions have been filled; Mr. Pagel indicated that two social worker positions are open, as well as one science teacher and two special education teacher positions still to be filled. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Board approve the personnel recommendations. Curriculum: summer learning. Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, shared a PowerPoint presentation on the District's Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update. The District held Principal Retreats and Teaching & Learning Department Retreats and offered the TSD Literacy Project, in which over 80 teachers participated. Student learning over the summer included Preschool Literacy and Mathematics Institutes; a free summer program for students entering grades 6-8 called the Summer Learning Lab, focused on deep learning using the Stanford design thinking process to undertake a project of the students' own choosing; Title 1 summer opportunities such as the Morse Summer Nights reading program, book clubs, and writing and art camp; summer programs for multilingual learners; high school summer school; and special education programs. There was no business item.

Public communication on non-agenda items. Mr. Alex Karpowitsch, Troy resident, addressed the Board about livestreaming Board of Education meetings and engaging in dialogue with community members who choose to speak during meetings, and also spoke about the recent publishing of test scores.

Board comments. Dr. Philippart thanked the new student reps and announced that the Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence (TFEE) is kicking off the new school year with a strategy session on providing new grant opportunities for teachers and students to enrich educational programs in the Troy School District. Mr. Haupt thanked the new student reps and wished them a safe and fun Homecoming. Mrs. Anne talked about Michigan legislation on diversifying religious holidays and expressed a desire to do the same in the district. Mrs. Alic welcomed everyone to a new school year, echoed Mrs. Anne in hoping that school calendars, not yet set, will reflect the holidays of the diverse Troy community, and spoke about suicide prevention and safety as a community effort to keep kids safe. Mr. Hauff congratulated board members on the MASB awards, noting the hard work and dedication required. Dr. Wilson gave a shout out to teachers for getting the school year off to a good start. Mr. West shared that the school year has been off to a great start, that Open Houses and Curriculum Nights are going well, that a community survey will be sent in the next couple of weeks to get feedback on the school calendar, and that the annual Fall Update to building staff and parent groups will begin soon. Mr. Schmidt recognized Ms. Montante, the new Director of Communications and Strategic Initiatives, on the quality of her communications, and discussed the M-Step scores and his frustration that they were released to the public prior to the district seeing them. He announced the next Board Workshop for October 3rd at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the next regular meeting for October 17th at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building.
